intro: Around 500 BCE, China was breaking apart. The Zhou kings had lost their power, and rival states fought for land and survival. Rulers wanted advice, and thinkers traveled from court to court to give it. This troubled age produced some of the most important philosophy in world history.

In this unit you will meet the Zhou and their Mandate of Heaven, Confucius on the road, and the Hundred Schools of Thought. You will read Mozi on caring for all and Han Feizi on reward and punishment. You will follow Qin's rise, the burning of the books, and the Han choice of Confucian learning.

By the end, you will be able to place the thinkers on a timeline and compare what each school taught. You will be able to tell a primary source from a later legend. And you will be able to explain how historians weigh a story like the burning of the books.
bigQuestion: How did war and rivalry among states shape the ideas that became the Chinese classics?

title: The Age of Philosophers

chapters.title: Zhou, Spring and Autumn and the Hundred Schools
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did an age of war and disorder produce so many great thinkers?

story.title: The Adviser on the Road
story.kicker: A teacher travels from court to court with his students, and no ruler will put his ideas to work.
paragraphs: The ox cart bumps along a dirt road. Inside sits a man in his fifties, with a handful of students walking beside him. He has left his home state of Lu. He is looking for a ruler who will listen. His name is Kong Qiu. Later ages will call him Kongzi, or Confucius.

At each court the pattern is the same. A duke greets him politely and asks for advice. Confucius talks about ruling by good example, about ritual and about caring for the people. The duke nods. Then he asks how to win his next war. Confucius has little to say about armies, and he soon moves on.

Some days go badly. Tradition tells that the group once ran out of food between two states, and some students grew angry. "Does a gentleman also face such hardship?" one asks. Confucius answers that a gentleman stays steady in hard times, while a small person loses control.

After about fourteen years on the road, Confucius returns home. He never gains the high office he hoped for. He spends his last years teaching. Yet his students will carry his words across China, and a book of his sayings, the Analects, will be read for over two thousand years.
story.think: Why might a teacher keep traveling and giving advice when no ruler takes it?

lessons.title: The Zhou Take Power
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhou dynasty overthrew the Shang and explained its rule with the idea of the Mandate of Heaven.
reading: Around 1046 BCE (traditional dates run earlier, to 1122 BCE), the Zhou people defeated the Shang kings at the Battle of Muye. The Zhou founded a *dynasty*, a line of rulers from one family. It lasted until 256 BCE, longer than any other in Chinese history.

The Zhou needed to explain why they had the right to rule. Their answer appears in the Book of Documents, one of the oldest Chinese texts. It says that Heaven (*tian*) gives the right to rule to a virtuous family. When a ruler becomes cruel and careless, Heaven takes that right away and gives it to another.

This idea is called the *Mandate of Heaven*. The Zhou said the last Shang king had been cruel, so Heaven had passed the mandate to them. Later Chinese dynasties used the same idea for about three thousand years, both to claim power and to judge rulers who failed.

words.d: a line of rulers from the same family who rule one after another
the idea that Heaven gives the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and can take it away
Heaven; in early Chinese texts, the high power that watches over rulers and the world

look.title: The Zhou Dynasty in Parts
rows: Western Zhou ends; capital moves east
look.cite: Standard dates, e.g. The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Zhou conquest and the end of the Zhou dynasty?

check.q: What does the Mandate of Heaven explain?
choices: Why a ruler has the right to rule and can lose it
check.why: The Mandate of Heaven says Heaven grants rule to virtuous rulers and removes it from cruel ones.

check.q: Which dynasty did the Zhou overthrow?
check.why: The Zhou defeated the Shang, c. 1046 BCE.

check.q: In which old text does the Mandate of Heaven appear?
check.why: Speeches in the Book of Documents explain the Zhou claim to Heaven's mandate.

lessons.title: The Duke of Zhou
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius admired the early Zhou, especially the Duke of Zhou, as a model of good government and ritual.
reading: After the Zhou conquest, the young king was too young to rule alone. His uncle, the *Duke of Zhou*, ruled for him. Tradition says the duke then handed power back when the king came of age. Tradition also credits him with setting the rules of court ritual and music.

Five centuries later, Confucius looked back at the early Zhou as a golden age. In Analects 7.5 he sighs that he has not dreamed of the Duke of Zhou for a long time, a sign to him that he was growing old. In Analects 3.14 he says the Zhou learned from the two dynasties before it, and so he follows the Zhou.

Historians note that much of this picture is idealized. The early Zhou fought wars and put down revolts. But for Confucius and his followers, the early Zhou stood for *ritual* order and rulers who led by virtue. That ideal shaped Confucian thinking.

words.d: an early Zhou leader who ruled for a young king; Confucius admired him as a model
a set of formal actions done in a set way, such as ceremonies, greetings and offerings
shown as better or more perfect than it really was

look.title: Following the Zhou
look.text: Chau had the advantage of viewing the two past dynasties. How complete and elegant are its regulations! I follow Chau.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 3.14, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Why does Confucius say he follows the Zhou (Legge spells it Chau)?

check.q: Why did the Duke of Zhou rule for a time?
choices: The young king was too young to rule alone
check.why: Tradition says the Duke of Zhou ruled for his young nephew and then returned power.

check.q: In Analects 3.14, which dynasty does Confucius say he follows?
check.why: Confucius says the Zhou learned from the two earlier dynasties, so he follows the Zhou.

check.q: What do historians say about Confucius's picture of the early Zhou?
check.why: Historians note the early Zhou also had wars and revolts; Confucius's picture is an ideal.

lessons.title: A Kingdom Breaks Apart
lessons.mainIdea: After 771 BCE the Zhou kings lost real power, and many states competed and fought through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.
reading: In 771 BCE, invaders and rebels killed a Zhou king, and the court fled east to Luoyang. From then on, Zhou kings kept their title and rituals but had little real power. Local lords ruled their own states and fought one another.

Historians divide the next centuries into two parts. The *Spring and Autumn period* (771–476 BCE) is named after a history of the state of Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals. The *Warring States period* (475–221 BCE) is named for its constant wars among seven large states.

Over time, small states were swallowed by larger ones. Armies grew to hundreds of thousands of soldiers. Rulers needed clever advisers to plan wars, collect taxes and run their lands. That need opened the door for a new kind of person: the traveling thinker.

words.d: 771–476 BCE, when the Zhou kings were weak and many states competed
475–221 BCE, when seven large states fought until Qin united China
here, a territory ruled by its own lord or king, like Lu, Qi or Qin

look.title: Weak King, Strong Lords
look.text: Picture a school where the principal still gives speeches and hands out awards, but no one follows the rules. Each grade makes its own laws. The biggest grades take over the smaller ones' rooms.
look.prompt: How is this like the Zhou after 771 BCE? Where does the comparison not fit?

check.q: What happened to Zhou kings after 771 BCE?
choices: They kept their title but lost real power
check.why: After the move east, Zhou kings kept rituals but local lords held real power.

check.q: Where does the name Spring and Autumn come from?
choices: A history of Lu, the Spring and Autumn Annals
check.why: The period is named for the Spring and Autumn Annals, a history of the state of Lu.

check.q: Which dates belong to the Warring States period?
check.why: The Warring States period runs from 475 to 221 BCE, when Qin unified China.

lessons.title: A Teacher from Lu
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius (traditional dates 551–479 BCE) was a teacher from the state of Lu who hoped to restore good order through virtue and ritual.
reading: Tradition dates Confucius's life to 551–479 BCE. He was born in the state of Lu, in what is now Shandong province. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu. The title *Kongzi* means Master Kong; Jesuit writers in the 1600s turned the longer form Kong Fuzi into the Latin Confucius.

According to later accounts, Confucius grew up poor and worked in small jobs, such as keeping granaries. He loved learning. The Analects reports him saying that at fifteen he set his heart on learning (2.4). He held some office in Lu, though scholars debate how high.

Confucius became famous as a teacher. Tradition says he taught students from rich and poor families alike. In Analects 7.7 he says he never refused to teach anyone who brought even a small gift. His students later spread his teachings and served in governments.

words.d: Master Kong, the Chinese title of Confucius
beliefs and stories passed down over time; traditional dates are those accepted by long custom
the collection of sayings of Confucius and his students, in 20 books

look.title: A Life in Stages
look.text: At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 2.4, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: What does Confucius say changed in him at each age? Why might a teacher describe his own growth?

check.q: What are Confucius's traditional dates?
check.why: Tradition dates Confucius's life to 551–479 BCE.

check.q: Where did the name Confucius come from?
check.why: Jesuit missionaries in the 1600s turned Kong Fuzi into the Latin form Confucius.

check.q: What did Confucius say in Analects 7.7?
choices: He never refused a student who brought a small gift
check.why: In 7.7 Confucius says he never refused instruction to anyone who came with even a small gift.

lessons.title: Looking for a Ruler
lessons.mainIdea: Like many thinkers of his time, Confucius traveled from state to state looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice.
reading: Around 497 BCE, according to Sima Qian's account, Confucius left Lu. For about fourteen years he traveled through states such as Wei, Chen and Cai. He met rulers and gave advice, but none gave him the power to reform their government.

The Analects records people who doubted him. In 14.38 (numbered 14.41 in Legge), a gatekeeper describes Confucius as the man who knows a thing cannot be done and still keeps doing it. In book 18, hermits tell his students that the world is a flood no one can stop, so why try.

Confucius was not alone. In the Warring States period many *advisers* moved from court to court. Rulers welcomed them because they wanted ideas that would make their states strong. Advisers hoped to find a ruler who would listen.

words.d: a person who gives advice to a ruler about how to govern
a person who lives apart from society, often for spiritual or moral reasons

look.title: The Gatekeeper's Words
look.text: A gatekeeper asks a student of Confucius where he comes from. When he hears the answer, he says: Is he not the one who knows it cannot be done, and keeps on doing it?
look.cite: Analects 14.38 (14.41 in Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1893), paraphrased
look.prompt: Is the gatekeeper praising or mocking Confucius? How could a reader argue each side?

check.q: Why did Confucius travel for about fourteen years?
choices: To find a ruler who would use his ideas
check.why: Confucius traveled among states seeking a ruler who would put his teachings into practice.

check.q: Who says Confucius knows a thing cannot be done yet keeps doing it?
check.why: In Analects 14.38 (14.41 in Legge), a gatekeeper describes Confucius this way.

check.q: Why did rulers welcome traveling advisers?
choices: They wanted ideas to make their states strong
check.why: In a time of competition and war, rulers sought advice that would strengthen their states.

lessons.title: Legends and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Historians separate what early sources show about Confucius from later legends that grew around him.
reading: Much of what people know about Confucius comes from two sources. One is the Analects, compiled by his students and their students over many years. The other is a biography in the Records of the Historian (*Shiji*) by Sima Qian, finished around 94 BCE, about four centuries after Confucius died.

A *primary source* is evidence from the time being studied. For Confucius, even the Analects was collected after his death, and scholars debate which parts are oldest. Sima Qian used older records, but he also included stories that historians cannot check.

Later ages added *legends*: that a unicorn-like qilin appeared at his birth, or that he edited all of the Five Classics. Legends matter because they show how people honored him. Historians simply label them as legend, not as proven fact.

words.d: evidence from the time being studied, such as a letter, inscription or record
Records of the Historian, a history of China by Sima Qian, finished c. 94 BCE
a story passed down about a person or event that cannot be proven

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim A: Confucius came from the state of Lu. Claim B: A qilin appeared when he was born. Claim C: His sayings were collected by students after his death. Claim D: He personally edited every one of the Five Classics.
look.prompt: Which claims are well supported by early sources, and which are later traditions? Explain how you decided.

check.q: Who wrote the Shiji, with its biography of Confucius?
check.why: Sima Qian finished the Records of the Historian around 94 BCE.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: Evidence from the time being studied
check.why: A primary source comes from the time being studied.

check.q: How do historians treat stories like the qilin at Confucius's birth?
choices: As legend that shows how people honored him
check.why: Historians label such stories as legend and study them for what they show about later honor.

lessons.title: Why Chaos Made Thinkers
lessons.mainIdea: War, change and competition among states led many thinkers to ask how people and states should be ordered.
reading: Why did so many philosophers appear in the Warring States period? Historians point to several causes. The old order of the Zhou had broken down, so people asked what should replace it. Rulers paid for good ideas. And writing spread beyond a small group of court officials.

The state of Qi even founded a center of learning, the *Jixia Academy*, around the 300s BCE. Scholars from many schools lived there on state support and debated. Mencius and Xunzi are both linked to Qi in the sources.

Thinkers argued about the same basic questions. How should a ruler govern? Is human nature good or bad? Should people follow ritual, law, love for all, or the natural Way? Their answers became the *Hundred Schools of Thought*. "Hundred" means many, not exactly one hundred.

words.d: the many schools of philosophy in China c. 500–221 BCE; hundred means many
a center of learning in the state of Qi where thinkers of many schools debated
the study of basic questions about how to live, know and govern

look.title: One Question, Many Answers
look.text: A ruler asks: "My state is in danger. What should I do?" Adviser 1: "Lead by good example and keep the rites." Adviser 2: "Write strict laws and punish anyone who breaks them." Adviser 3: "Stop fighting, and care for all people equally." Adviser 4: "Do less. Stop forcing things."
look.prompt: Which answer sounds most like each school you will meet in this section? What does each assume about people?

check.q: What does 'hundred' mean in Hundred Schools of Thought?
check.why: The phrase means many schools, not a precise count.

check.q: What was the Jixia Academy?
choices: A center of learning in Qi
check.why: The Jixia Academy in Qi supported scholars from many schools who debated there.

check.q: Which is one reason historians give for the rise of the Hundred Schools?
choices: The Zhou order had broken down, and rulers wanted new ideas
China was at peace for centuries
check.why: The collapse of Zhou order and competition among states created demand for new ideas.

lessons.title: Confucians and Daoists
lessons.mainIdea: Confucians taught virtue, ritual and learning, while Daoists taught following the natural Way and acting without forcing.
reading: The *Confucians* (in Chinese, the Ru, or scholars) followed Confucius. They taught that society becomes orderly when people practice *ren*, humane care for others, and *li*, ritual and proper conduct. Rulers, they said, should lead by moral example, and people should keep learning all their lives.

The *Daoists* are named for the *Dao*, the Way. The Daodejing, a short poetic book linked to Laozi, says the Dao cannot be fully put into words. It praises *wu wei*, often translated as "non-action" or acting without forcing. The Zhuangzi adds funny stories and puzzles.

The two schools disagreed. The Daodejing, ch. 18, suggests that talk of humaneness and rightness appears only after the great Way is lost. Confucians answered that people need learning and ritual to grow. Yet many Chinese readers later drew on both.

words.d: humaneness; caring for others; the highest virtue in Confucius's teaching
ritual and proper conduct, from ceremonies to everyday manners
the Way; in the Daodejing, the source and pattern of all things
acting without forcing, sometimes translated as non-action; a key Daoist idea

look.title: When the Great Way Is Lost
look.text: When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.
look.cite: Daodejing ch. 18, trans. James Legge, The Tao Teh King, Sacred Books of the East 39 (1891)
look.prompt: What is the Daodejing suggesting about Confucian virtues here? How might a Confucian reply?

check.q: Which term means humane care for others in Confucius's teaching?
check.why: Ren is humaneness, the central Confucian virtue.

check.q: What does wu wei mean?
check.why: Wu wei, a Daoist idea, means acting without forcing, or non-action.

check.q: What does Daodejing ch. 18 suggest?
choices: Ritual is the source of the Way
Talk of benevolence appears after the Way is lost
check.why: Chapter 18 says benevolence and righteousness came into vogue when the great Way was no longer followed.

lessons.title: Mohists and Legalists
lessons.mainIdea: Mohists taught care for all and opposed aggressive war; Legalists taught strict laws, rewards and punishments.
reading: The *Mohists* followed Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE). He taught *jian ai*, often translated "universal love" or impartial care: caring for other people's families and states as for your own. Mohists opposed attacking wars and spending too much on funerals and music.

The *Legalists* took a very different view. Thinkers like Shang Yang and Han Feizi argued that people act mainly for reward and to avoid punishment. So a ruler should make clear laws, enforce them strictly, and reward farming and fighting. The state of Qin used these ideas and grew strong.

Historian Sima Tan, father of Sima Qian, later sorted the thinkers into six schools, including Confucians, Daoists, Mohists and Legalists. Scholars today note these labels were made after the fact. Many thinkers borrowed from more than one.

words.d: followers of Mozi, who taught impartial care for all and opposed aggressive war
impartial care or universal love; Mozi's teaching to care for all people equally
thinkers such as Han Feizi who taught strict law, reward and punishment

look.title: Rough Dates of Key Thinkers
look.cite: Common scholarly estimates; exact dates are uncertain
look.prompt: Which thinkers lived closest in time? Who could have heard of Confucius's teachings already written down?

check.q: What did Mozi teach?
choices: Impartial care for all and opposition to aggressive war
check.why: Mozi taught jian ai, care for all, and opposed attacking wars.

check.q: What did Legalists believe drove people?
check.why: Legalists like Han Feizi held that people respond mainly to reward and punishment.

check.q: Who sorted early thinkers into six schools?
check.why: Sima Tan, father of Sima Qian, named six schools; scholars note the labels came later.

lessons.title: Reading an Old Debate
lessons.mainIdea: The schools answered each other, so each one is easier to understand beside its rivals.
reading: The Hundred Schools did not think alone. Mencius, a Confucian, attacked Mozi's teaching of equal love, saying it ignored special duties to one's own father. Han Feizi, a Legalist, mocked Confucians for praising ancient kings in a changed world.

Mencius also met rulers who wanted quick gains. In Mencius 1A.1, King Hui of Liang asks how Mencius can *profit* his kingdom. Mencius replies that he brings only humaneness and rightness; if everyone seeks profit, the kingdom will be in danger.

Reading these *debates* helps you see what each school cared about most. A Confucian stressed family and virtue. A Mohist stressed fairness to all. A Legalist stressed order and power. A Daoist questioned all of their busy plans.

words.d: an argument in which people give reasons for different views
gain or advantage; Mencius criticized rulers who put profit first

look.title: Why Speak of Profit?
look.text: King Hui asks Mencius what he has brought to profit the kingdom. Mencius asks why the king must speak of profit. He says he brings only humaneness and rightness, and warns that if ruler and people all seek profit, the state will be in danger.
look.cite: Mencius 1A.1, paraphrased from James Legge, The Works of Mencius, The Chinese Classics vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1895)
look.prompt: What does Mencius think will happen if everyone seeks profit? How might a Legalist answer him?

check.q: What did Mencius criticize about Mozi's teaching?
choices: It was too strict about law
It ignored special duties to one's own family
check.why: Mencius said Mozi's equal love ignored the special bond with one's own father.

check.q: In Mencius 1A.1, what does King Hui want?
check.why: King Hui asks how Mencius can profit his kingdom; Mencius answers with humaneness and rightness.

check.q: Which school questioned all the others' busy plans?
check.why: Daoist texts question ambitious plans and praise acting without forcing.

review.why: Confucius looked to the Duke of Zhou as a model of ritual and good rule (Analects 7.5).

review.why: The qilin story is a later legend; the others are supported by early sources.

choices: Laozi and the Mandate of Heaven
review.why: Mozi taught jian ai, impartial care for all.

review.q: Why did many advisers travel between courts?
choices: They sought rulers who would use their ideas
review.why: Competing rulers wanted advice, and thinkers looked for a ruler who would listen.

review.q: What does Daodejing ch. 18 suggest about benevolence and righteousness?
choices: They are the source of the Way

chapters.title: Mozi, the Legalists and the Burning of the Books
chapters.bigQuestion: What happens to ideas when rival schools compete for a ruler's power?

story.title: Books in the Wall
story.kicker: A minister orders the old books burned, and a scholar hides his copy where no one will look.
paragraphs: The year is 213 BCE. The Qin state has conquered all its rivals, and its king now calls himself the First Emperor. At court, a scholar praises the ancient kings and says the emperor should follow their ways. The chief minister, Li Si, is angry.

Li Si tells the emperor that scholars use old books to criticize the present. He proposes an order. Histories of other states are to be burned. Private copies of the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents must be handed over. Books on medicine, divination and farming may be kept. The emperor agrees.

In the east, according to the historian Sima Qian, a scholar named Fu Sheng knows the Book of Documents well. He does not want it lost. He hides his copy inside a wall of his house. Then war and rebellion sweep the land, and he flees.

Years later, after the Qin has fallen, Fu Sheng returns home. He breaks open the wall. Many bamboo strips are gone, but some chapters survive. As an old man he teaches them, and the Han court sends a scholar to learn from him. Part of an ancient book lives on.
story.think: Why would a new government want to control which books people could read?

lessons.title: Caring for All Equally
lessons.mainIdea: Mozi taught that the world's troubles come from partial care and would end if people cared for others as they care for their own.
reading: Mozi (c. 470–391 BCE) lived soon after Confucius. Tradition says he first studied Confucian teachings, then broke away. The book called the *Mozi* collects his teachings and those of his followers.

The Mozi's chapters on *jian ai*, impartial care, ask where disorder comes from. Their answer: people care for themselves, their own families and their own states, and harm others for their gain. If people cared for others' families and states as for their own, thieves, feuds and wars would stop.

Confucians disagreed. They taught *graded* love, starting with one's own parents and spreading outward. Mencius called Mozi's teaching a denial of one's father. Mohists replied that caring for others' parents is the surest way to have your own parents cared for.

words.d: a thinker (c. 470–391 BCE) who taught impartial care; also the book of his school
impartial care, often called universal love; care for others as for your own
the Confucian view that care begins with family and spreads outward in degrees

look.title: Where Disorder Comes From
look.text: If people regarded other people's states as their own, who would attack them? If they regarded other people's families as their own, who would disturb them? So impartial care brings order, and partial care brings disorder.
look.cite: Mozi, 'Impartial Care' (Jian Ai) chapters 14–16, paraphrased; see Burton Watson, Mo Tzu: Basic Writings (1963)
look.prompt: What cause of war does the Mozi name? Do you think a Confucian would accept this reasoning? Why or why not?

check.q: What does jian ai mean?
check.why: Jian ai is Mozi's teaching of caring for others as for one's own.

check.q: How did Confucians view love?
check.why: Confucians taught graded love beginning with parents and extending outward.

check.q: Which thinker criticized Mozi's teaching as denying one's father?
check.why: Mencius attacked Mozi's equal love as ignoring the special duty to one's father.

lessons.title: Against War and Waste
lessons.mainIdea: Mohists opposed aggressive war and costly funerals and music, and they judged actions by whether they benefit the people.
reading: The Mozi argues against offensive war. It points out that stealing a peach is called wrong, and killing one person is called a crime. Yet when a state kills thousands in an attack, people praise it. The book calls this a failure to tell right from wrong.

Mohists also criticized *extravagance*. Long mourning periods and rich funerals, which Confucians valued as ritual, wasted wealth and kept people from work. Grand court music used resources that could feed the poor. Mohists judged each practice by its *benefit* to the people.

Confucians replied that rites and music shape feeling and bind families and communities. The Mohists also taught that Heaven wishes people to care for one another, and that spirits reward good and punish evil. The two schools shared some ideas and argued over others.

words.d: spending far more than is needed
what helps people; Mohists judged every practice by whether it benefits the people

look.title: Weighing a Funeral
look.text: A family spends its savings on a grand funeral and mourns for three years. A Confucian says: this honors a parent and teaches respect. A Mohist says: this wastes food and work the living need.
look.prompt: What value does each speaker put first? Describe both views without choosing one.

check.q: What comparison does the Mozi use against war?
choices: Killing thousands is praised while killing one is called a crime
check.why: The Mozi contrasts calling small wrongs crimes with praising the mass killing of war.

check.q: Why did Mohists criticize rich funerals?
choices: They wasted wealth needed by the living
check.why: Mohists judged practices by benefit and saw costly funerals as waste.

check.q: How did Confucians defend ritual and music?
choices: As shaping feeling and binding communities
check.why: Confucians held that rites and music shape character and bind families.

lessons.title: Mozi Walks to Chu
lessons.mainIdea: A famous story shows Mohists acting on their beliefs by defending small states from attack.
reading: The Mozi chapter called "Gongshu" tells a story. The engineer Gongshu Ban had built new siege ladders for the large state of Chu, which planned to attack the small state of Song. Mozi heard the news and, the story says, walked for ten days and nights to reach Chu.

Mozi first argued that attacking Song was wrong. Then he held a model contest with Gongshu Ban, using his belt as a city wall and small sticks as machines. Nine times Gongshu Ban attacked; nine times Mozi defended. The king of Chu called off the attack.

The story shows why Mohists became known as *defense* experts. They studied walls and siege methods to protect small states. Scholars read the tale as a teaching story. It shows the school's ideal: care for others, backed by skill and action.

words.d: surrounding and attacking a walled city
protecting a place or people from attack

look.title: Belt and Sticks
look.text: Picture two men kneeling on a palace floor. One lays his belt in a circle for a city wall. The other moves small wooden sticks as siege towers and ladders. Again and again the attacker moves; again and again the defender blocks. The king watches.
look.prompt: Why might the storytellers have Mozi win with a model instead of a real battle? What does that say about Mohist values?

check.q: Which state did Chu plan to attack in the story?
check.why: In the Gongshu chapter, Chu planned to attack the small state of Song.

check.q: How did Mozi stop the attack in the story?
choices: He argued and then beat Gongshu Ban in a model contest
check.why: Mozi argued against the attack and defended nine times in a model contest.

check.q: What were Mohists known for?
check.why: Mohists studied defense to protect small states from attack.

lessons.title: Law, Reward and Punishment
lessons.mainIdea: Han Feizi taught that a ruler keeps order through clear laws and the 'two handles' of reward and punishment.
reading: Han Feizi (c. 280–233 BCE) was a prince of the small state of Han. Tradition says he studied with the Confucian Xunzi. Yet he drew very different conclusions. His book, the *Han Feizi*, gathers the ideas later called *Legalism*.

In the chapter "The Two Handles," Han Feizi says a ruler controls officials with two handles: reward and punishment. People like reward and fear punishment, so a wise ruler uses both. Laws must be public, clear and the same for everyone, noble or poor.

Han Feizi mocked rulers who waited for a sage king. He compared them to a farmer in the state of Song. A rabbit once ran into a tree stump and broke its neck. The farmer then gave up plowing and waited by the stump for another rabbit.

words.d: a later name for the school of Han Feizi and Shang Yang, which stressed law, reward and punishment
a thinker (c. 280–233 BCE) who taught Legalist ideas; also his book
Han Feizi's name for reward and punishment, the ruler's tools of control

look.title: Waiting by the Stump
look.text: A farmer of Song saw a rabbit run into a stump and break its neck. He put down his plow and waited by the stump for another rabbit. He never caught one, and all of Song laughed at him. Rulers who try to govern today by the ways of ancient kings are like this farmer.
look.cite: Han Feizi ch. 49, 'The Five Vermin,' paraphrased; see Burton Watson, Han Fei Tzu: Basic Writings (1964)
look.prompt: Whom is Han Feizi criticizing with this story? How might a Confucian answer?

check.q: What are Han Feizi's 'two handles'?
check.why: Han Feizi names reward and punishment as the ruler's two handles.

check.q: Whom does the stump story criticize?
check.why: Han Feizi mocks rulers who govern by ancient models, like the farmer waiting for a rabbit.

check.q: What kind of laws did Han Feizi want?
choices: Public, clear and the same for all
check.why: Han Feizi taught that laws must be clear, public and applied equally.

lessons.title: Qin Unites China
lessons.mainIdea: Using Legalist methods, the state of Qin conquered its rivals and in 221 BCE created China's first empire.
reading: In the 350s BCE, the minister Shang Yang reformed the state of Qin. He rewarded farmers and soldiers, grouped families to watch one another, and set harsh punishments. Qin grew rich and strong. By 221 BCE its king had conquered the other six large states.

The king took a new title, Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. His minister Li Si helped him *standardize* the realm: one way of writing characters, one set of weights and measures, one width for cart axles and one kind of coin. Workers joined older walls in the north and built roads.

Historians still weigh this *unification*. It created a single state and a shared script that lasted. It also relied on heavy labor, harsh laws and war. The Qin dynasty itself lasted only about fifteen years.

words.d: joining separate states into one
make things the same everywhere, like weights, coins or writing
the First Emperor of Qin, who united China in 221 BCE

look.title: The Rise and Fall of Qin
look.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 6; standard dates
look.prompt: How many years passed between unification and the fall of Qin? What does that suggest?

check.q: In what year did Qin unify China?
check.why: Qin completed its conquest of the other states in 221 BCE.

check.q: Which minister helped the First Emperor standardize writing and measures?
check.why: Li Si guided the standardization of script, weights and measures.

check.q: About how long did the Qin dynasty last?
check.why: Qin lasted from 221 to 206 BCE, about fifteen years.

lessons.title: The Burning of the Books
lessons.mainIdea: Sima Qian reports that in 213 BCE Qin ordered many books burned; historians debate how much was lost and how accurate later accounts are.
reading: Sima Qian's Shiji tells that in 213 BCE Li Si proposed burning histories of other states and private copies of the Songs, the Documents and the writings of the schools. Books on medicine, divination and farming were spared. Copies were kept in the imperial library for official scholars.

The Shiji adds that in 212 BCE the emperor had more than 460 scholars killed. For centuries, Confucian writers remembered Qin as the great enemy of learning. The phrase "burning books and burying scholars" became a warning against *censorship*.

Modern historians weigh the evidence. Some note that Han-era writers had reasons to paint Qin badly. Others point out that more books may have been lost when rebels burned the Qin palace in 206 BCE. Most agree the order was real and that it harmed the *transmission* of old texts.

words.d: a government controlling or banning what people can read, write or say
the passing down of a text from copy to copy and teacher to student
chief minister of Qin who proposed the book-burning order

look.title: Two Historians, One Event
look.text: Historian A: "Sima Qian lived under the Han, who replaced Qin. The Han wanted Qin to look cruel, so we should read his account carefully." Historian B: "The order is also recorded as Li Si's own proposal, with details on which books were spared. That detail suggests a real policy."
look.prompt: What evidence does each historian use? How can both points be partly true?

check.q: Which books did the Qin order spare?
check.why: Sima Qian reports that practical books on medicine, divination and farming were spared.

check.q: Why do some historians read Sima Qian's account carefully?
choices: He lived under the Han, who had reasons to paint Qin badly
check.why: As a Han historian, Sima Qian wrote for a dynasty that replaced Qin.

check.q: What other event may have destroyed many books?
choices: The founding of the Jixia Academy
Rebels burning the Qin palace in 206 BCE
check.why: Many historians note that the burning of the Qin palace library in 206 BCE may have caused great losses.

lessons.title: Recovering Lost Books
lessons.mainIdea: Under the Han, scholars recovered the classics from memory and hidden copies, which led to different versions of some texts.
reading: After Qin fell, the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) lifted the ban on books in 191 BCE. Scholars set to work recovering the classics. Fu Sheng, according to Sima Qian, taught the surviving chapters of the Book of Documents. They were written down in the new clerical script of the day.

Later, Han accounts say, workers tearing down a wall of Confucius's old house in Qufu found texts written in an older script. These became known as the *Old Text* versions. The versions taught from memory and newer copies were called *New Text*.

Scholars argued for centuries over which versions were more reliable. Some Old Text chapters of the Documents, later scholars showed, were forgeries from after the Han. This history is why careful study of *manuscripts* matters.

words.d: versions of the classics said to be found in older script, such as in Confucius's house wall
versions of the classics passed down by Han teachers and written in Han script
a handwritten copy of a text

look.title: Two Copies Disagree
look.text: Scholar 1 learned a text from an old teacher who recited it from memory. Scholar 2 has bamboo strips pulled from a wall, written in an older script that few can read. The two copies differ in some words and chapters.
look.prompt: What are the strengths and weaknesses of each copy? How might a careful scholar decide between them?

check.q: Who taught the surviving Book of Documents, according to Sima Qian?
check.why: Sima Qian reports that Fu Sheng hid and later taught the Documents.

check.q: What were Old Text versions?
choices: Texts in older script, said to be found in Confucius's house wall
check.why: Old Text versions were written in pre-Qin script, reportedly found in a wall of Confucius's house.

check.q: What did later scholars show about some Old Text Documents chapters?
choices: They were forgeries from after the Han
check.why: Scholars proved some Old Text Documents chapters were later forgeries.

lessons.title: Confucian Learning Becomes Official
lessons.mainIdea: Under Emperor Wu, the Han court made the Confucian classics the core of official learning.
reading: Early Han rulers borrowed from many schools. Some favored Daoist ideas of light government. Qin-style laws also stayed in use. But under Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE), the court gave special status to Confucian learning.

In 136 BCE the court set up posts for *erudites*, official scholars, of the Five Classics. In 124 BCE it founded the *Imperial Academy* to train future officials in them. The scholar Dong Zhongshu urged the emperor to favor Confucian teachings, and Han histories give him credit for the change.

Historians note that the Han state stayed a mix. It used Confucian language about virtue and ritual, along with strict laws that owed much to Legalism. Some describe the result as Confucian on the outside and Legalist within.

words.d: a school founded in 124 BCE to train Han officials in the Confucian classics
an official scholar appointed to teach one of the classics
Han emperor (r. 141–87 BCE) under whom Confucian learning became official

look.title: Confucian Learning in the Han
rows: Posts for erudites of Five Classics
look.cite: Standard dates, e.g. The Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
look.prompt: How long after the Qin fall did the Han create posts for the Five Classics?

check.q: Under which emperor did Confucian learning become official?
check.why: Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE) gave Confucian learning official status.

check.q: What was the Imperial Academy?
choices: A school to train officials in the classics
check.why: Founded in 124 BCE, it trained future officials in the Confucian classics.

check.q: What do historians mean by 'Confucian outside, Legalist within'?
choices: The Han used Confucian ideals along with strict laws
check.why: Han government mixed Confucian language with Legalist-style law.

lessons.title: Why the Rivals Still Matter
lessons.mainIdea: The classics took shape in debate, so their rivals help readers understand what they argue.
reading: Mohism faded as a school after the Qin and Han, though parts of its thinking lived on. Legalist methods stayed in Chinese government. Daoism grew in new forms. Confucian learning became official. But each classic still carries traces of the old debates.

When the Analects stresses virtue over punishment, readers can hear the argument against Legalism. In Analects 2.3, Confucius says that people led by laws and punishments try to avoid penalties but have no *shame*. People led by virtue and ritual have a sense of shame and set themselves right.

Modern readers study the rivals for their own sake too. Some compare Mozi's impartial care to later ideas of universal rights. Others compare Han Feizi to European thinkers on power. Reading the rivals side by side shows what each *school* chose.

words.d: an inner sense of having done wrong, which Confucius believed guides good conduct
here, a group of thinkers who share a teacher or set of ideas

look.title: Laws or Virtue?
look.text: If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.
look.cite: Confucius, Analects 2.3, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (2nd ed., 1893)
look.prompt: Which rival school is this passage most at odds with? What does Confucius think law alone cannot do?

check.q: In Analects 2.3, what do people led only by punishment lack?
check.why: Confucius says people led by punishments avoid penalties but have no sense of shame.

check.q: Which school's ideas stayed in Chinese government after the Qin?
check.why: Legalist-style law continued in Chinese government even as Confucian learning became official.

check.q: Which rival is Analects 2.3 most at odds with?
check.why: Analects 2.3 favors virtue and ritual over rule by punishment, the Legalist method.

lessons.title: Weighing the Qin Story
lessons.mainIdea: Readers across history have used the Qin book burning as a lesson, and historians keep testing the story against evidence.
reading: For two thousand years, writers pointed to Qin to argue that rulers should respect scholars. The Han scholar Jia Yi wrote an essay, "The Faults of Qin," saying Qin fell because it ruled by force and did not show humaneness.

Archaeology has added evidence. In 1975, Qin legal texts on bamboo were found in a tomb at Shuihudi in Hubei. They show detailed laws and careful record-keeping. The Qin was harsh, but it was also highly organized. Evidence like this helps historians test the old story.

In the twentieth century, readers argued over Qin again. Some praised the First Emperor as a unifier. Others saw a warning about state power. Studying these readings shows how *history* is always read through the concerns of later times.

words.d: the study of the past through objects and sites people left behind
the study of the past and how people have told and interpreted it

look.title: A Tomb Full of Laws
look.text: In 1975, workers in Shuihudi, Hubei, opened the tomb of a Qin local official. Beside him lay over a thousand bamboo strips. They listed laws on farming, granaries, theft and the work of officials, with exact penalties.
look.prompt: What can these strips tell historians that Sima Qian's Shiji cannot? What can't they tell?

check.q: What did Jia Yi's essay 'The Faults of Qin' argue?
choices: Qin fell because it ruled by force without humaneness
check.why: Jia Yi said Qin fell because it relied on force and lacked humaneness.

check.q: What was found at Shuihudi in 1975?
check.why: A Qin official's tomb at Shuihudi held bamboo strips recording Qin laws.

check.q: Why do readers disagree about Qin?
choices: There is no evidence at all
Each age reads history through its own concerns
check.why: Different eras have praised or condemned Qin depending on their own concerns and evidence.

review.why: Mozi's followers taught jian ai and opposed offensive war.

review.why: Han Feizi's chapter 'The Two Handles' names reward and punishment.

review.q: In what year does Sima Qian date the order to burn books?
review.why: The Shiji dates Li Si's book-burning proposal to 213 BCE.

review.why: Sima Qian says Fu Sheng hid the Documents and later taught what survived.
The Han founded the Imperial Academy in 124 BCE to teach the classics.

choices: Rites shape feeling and bind families

review.q: What does Analects 2.3 say about ruling by punishment?
